extracted.intended_audience: EPA rulemakers, state regulators, utility attorneys, and rural electric cooperative stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Formal legal and policy comments submitted by the National Rural Electric Cooperative Association responding to EPA's Proposed Rule under Clean Air Act Section 111(d), critiquing statutory authority, technical assumptions (Building Blocks), implementation timelines, reliability impacts, and specific requested topics for comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability assumptions for nuclear and renewable generation (Building Block 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s assumptions in Building Block 3 concerning the availability of nuclear and renewable generation are neither supported by the docket nor practice, and are otherwise arbitrary and capricious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion asserts that assumptions must be supported by the record and consistent with industry practice; unsupported or conclusory assumptions render the rule arbitrary and capricious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost allocation and transmission needs for additional renewable generation
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s failure to address cost allocation of additional renewable generation and resulting transmission needs affords no opportunity for meaningful comment, and is otherwise arbitrary and capricious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory analyses must identify who bears costs for generation and transmission and allow meaningful notice-and-comment on allocation; omission undermines validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statewide availability assumptions for new renewable generation
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s assumptions concerning the availability of new renewable generation on a statewide basis are contrary to practice, unsupported by the record, and indicative of EPA’s failure to correctly interpret its own data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State-level deployment assumptions must reflect actual deployment practice and correct interpretation of EPA/EIA data; blanket statewide assumptions are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to account for additional intermediate generation to balance renewables
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s failure to account for necessary additional intermediate generation to balance added renewable generation is arbitrary and capricious, and renders the proposed scheme unworkable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modeling/BSER must account for grid-balancing resources (intermediate generation) required when adding variable renewables; omission makes the scheme impracticable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of who builds renewable generation and states' legal authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposal arbitrarily and capriciously ignores the fact that most renewable generation is not built by entities regulated by this proposal and that States have no legal authority to force additional investment in renewable generation without additional legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory obligations premised on assumed investment must consider whether regulated entities control such investment and whether states have legal authority to mandate it; failing to do so is arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of nuclear power within Building Block 3
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposal’s treatment of nuclear power generation irrationally treats nuclear power different than other sources that comprise Building Block 3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency in how generation technologies are treated in BSER is required; singling out nuclear for different treatment without justification is improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentives for 'at-risk' nuclear generating capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s treatment of 'at risk' nuclear generating capacity does not create a true incentive for owners of these facilities to keep them operating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If regulatory design purports to incentivize continued operation, the incentives must be structured to actually change owners’ economic decisions; mere labeling as 'at-risk' is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Future compliance risk for dispatchable zero-emission EGUs (nuclear)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dispatchable zero-emission EGUs (i.e., nuclear) have an inherent future risk of compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory analysis must account for regulatory/compliance risks that affect dispatchable zero-emission units' viability and economic decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for hydropower variability and potential diminishment
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposal’s failure to account for ongoing variability of hydropower and the potential for permanent hydropower diminishment due to new environmental constraints is arbitrary and capricious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hydropower should be modeled with its variability and susceptibility to regulatory/environmental constraints; assuming static availability is unreliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency in hydropower accounting with other renewables
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s accounting for hydropower conflicts with the treatment of other renewable energy and is arbitrary and capricious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodologies for crediting or accounting for different zero- or low-emitting resources must be consistent or well-justified when they differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority limits for end-use energy efficiency (Building Block 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Proposed Rule’s end-use energy efficiency requirements exceed both EPA’s authority and the authority of most state environmental agencies, and their inclusion in the underlying rule analysis and justification of the emissions targets undermines the entire rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA may not rely on measures outside its statutory authority (or state agencies' authority) as elements of BSER; inclusion of such measures invalidates target-setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity of including end-use energy efficiency as BSER
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s analysis underlying Building Block 4 is flawed, arbitrary, and capricious, and therefore the inclusion of end-use energy efficiency as an element of BSER for purposes of setting emission rate goals is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses supporting inclusion of measures in BSER must be rigorous and non-arbitrary; flawed analysis invalidates the measure’s use in setting goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of time for States' plan submissions and compliance date
rubrics_metrics.description: The time proposed for States’ submissions is too short, and the final compliance date should be extended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementation timelines must allow States adequate time for planning and stakeholder processes; unreasonably short deadlines may be procedurally and substantively problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of stringent interim goals on flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s establishment of stringent interim goals undermines any flexibility for States or utilities to comply with the requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interim goals should preserve reasonable compliance flexibility; overly strict interim requirements can impede practicable compliance and reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of historical implementation practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The Proposed Rule’s tight implementation deadlines ignore forty-four years of Clean Air Act history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule timing and transitional expectations should be informed by historical norms and precedent under the Clean Air Act; ignoring that history is a flaw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability impacts of retaining interim compliance goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliability will be threatened if EPA Retains the Interim Compliance Goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reliability impacts must be assessed and mitigated; retention of certain interim goals without safeguards may threaten grid reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Must identify nature and scope of federal implementation plans (FIPs)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA should identify in this rulemaking both the nature and the scope of the federal implementation plans it would prescribe where a State fails to submit a satisfactory plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notice-and-comment should include concrete descriptions of potential FIP remedies so States can meaningfully comment on consequences of inadequate plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory taking concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s proposal would constitute a regulatory taking for which compensation would be required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a regulation effects a taking under constitutional standards, agency must address takings implications and potential compensation; failure to do so raises legal infirmities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for a dynamic reliability safety valve
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must adopt a dynamic reliability safety valve that provides the States the flexibility they need to ensure reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule design should include adaptive mechanisms (safety valves) responsive to changing reliability conditions to avoid unintended grid disruptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation of rate-based CO2 goals to mass-based equivalents — guidance vs requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s proposed methods can only serve as guidance to states and not requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conversion methods provided by EPA should be treated as advisory; EPA cannot unilaterally impose mass-based equivalents as binding on States without statutory authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of proposed translation methods with rate-based methods
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA proposed methods are inconsistent with methods utilized to determine state rate-based goals and are otherwise arbitrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translation methodologies must be consistent with methods used to set rate goals; inconsistent conversions create arbitrariness and legal risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA cannot mandate tonnage rates for new fossil fuel sources
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA cannot mandate tonnage rates for new fossil fuel sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory limits prevent EPA from imposing mass (tonnage) standards for new sources beyond what Clean Air Act provision authorizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to EPA’s specific requested topics (aggregate rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA solicits comments on many discrete topics (e.g., Five Year Alternative; Monitoring and Compliance of Performance Goals; Trading Programs; Combining Two Source Categories; Enforcement Beyond EGUs; Using Section 110 Approval Mechanisms; Exception From New Source Review Program; Goal Calculation; Alternative Calculations; NGCC Data in Re-dispatch; Multi-State Goals; Five-Year Alternative; Emission Reduction Beyond Proposed Goals; Substitution by New NGCC EGU; Emission levels exceeding New Fossil-Fuel Fired EGU NSPS; Additional Agency Guidance; Reductions Concurrent with and before the Plan; RE and Demand-Side EE in a Rate-Based Plan; RE and Demand-Side Evaluation, Monitoring, and Verification; RE and Demand-Side EE Reporting Obligations; Emission Reduction Affecting Multiple States; Compliance Averaging Time; Goal Performance Tracking; Multi-year Format for Performance Goals; Compliance Record Retention; Offsetting RE and EE with Equivalent Fossil Reductions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each listed topic is a policy/technical dimension where EPA must provide rigorous analysis, legal authority, workable procedures, and opportunities for meaningful comment. Comments should address statutory authority, technical feasibility, allocation/reporting, verification, enforcement, interstate effects, and reliability for each topic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 111(d) prohibition on double-regulating source categories under Section 112
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 111(d) expressly prohibits double-regulating source categories already regulated under Section 112.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the statute and Supreme Court guidance, EPA may not use §111(d) to regulate pollutants from a source category already subject to §112 regulation; invoking §111(d) in that circumstance renders the rule unlawful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of House substantive amendment vs Senate conforming amendment (1990 Amendments)
rubrics_metrics.description: The substantive House amendment of Section 111(d) nullifies the Senate conforming amendment; the Senate amendment was clerical and should not be given substantive effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a substantive amendment and a conforming/clerical amendment conflict, longstanding rules of legislative draftsmanship and judicial practice direct treating the conforming amendment as a clerical mistake and give effect to the substantive amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting-error/scrivener's-error principle in statutory construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a failure to delete an inappropriate cross-reference or a simultaneous clerical change conflicts with substantive provisions, courts treat it as a drafting mistake and do not rewrite statute language to create an ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies and courts should not give substantive effect to obvious clerical errors in enacted statutes; doing so would contravene precedent and drafting norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevron framework for evaluating agency statutory interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether an agency’s interpretation of a statute is valid, courts employ Chevron: (1) whether Congress has spoken to the precise question; (2) if ambiguous, whether ambiguity is product of implicit delegation to agency; if not, afford only Skidmore deference; if yes, defer under Chevron step two only if interpretation is reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency interpretations must pass Chevron analysis; mere ambiguity does not automatically justify Chevron deference, and agencies may not rewrite clear statutory terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on agency reinterpretation when statute's language is clear
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency may not rewrite clear statutory terms to suit its own sense of how the statute should operate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where statutory language is unambiguous, courts will enforce the statute as written and decline to defer to agency reinterpretation that contradicts clear text.
